h1: Southern Cross hops for lemon and pine in pale ales
title: Southern Cross Hops for Lemon and Pine | Craft Beer School
desc: A New Zealand dual purpose hop with a lemon, pine and spice aroma. What it tastes like and how to use it in a 20 litre pale ale.
teaser: A New Zealand hop that smells of lemon zest and pine needles. It is a gentle way into pale ale hopping.
standfirst: Southern Cross is a New Zealand hop with a clean lemon, pine and spice profile. It bitters well and gives a pale ale a fresh, zesty finish without tropical fruit.
sections: A New Zealand hop that does two jobs

Southern Cross is a dual purpose hop from New Zealand, grown for both bittering and aroma. Alpha acids sit in the low teens in most lots, which makes it efficient in the kettle. The aroma is where homebrewers notice it: lemon peel, a resinous pine note and a pinch of spice.

That profile is closer to a classic pale ale than to the fruit-salad tropical hops that arrived later. If you want a pale ale that tastes fresh and crisp rather than juicy, Southern Cross is a sensible choice.
Where the lemon and pine come from

Every hop carries essential oils. Different oils smell of different things. Citrus notes come largely from terpene alcohols and related compounds. Pine and resin come from other terpenes. Southern Cross carries a mix that leans towards lemon and pine over tropical fruit. The proportion shifts with harvest and storage.

These oils are volatile. They go into the air if you boil them for an hour. For aroma you want the hop in contact with wort that is already off the heat, or with finished beer.
A 20 litre pale ale with Southern Cross

Target an original gravity near 1.050 and 35 IBU. A grist of 90% pale malt and 10% Munich gives a clean, slightly bready base. Mash at 66 °C for 60 minutes.

  • 60 minutes: 12 g of Southern Cross at 13% alpha. At 28% utilisation that gives 12 x 0.13 x 0.28 x 1,000 / 20 = 21.8 mg/L, so about 22 IBU.
  • 10 minutes: 15 g, for roughly 8 IBU more.
  • Whirlpool at 80 °C for 15 minutes: 30 g.
  • Dry hop for four days at 18 °C: 40 g.

The numbers are an estimate. Your real bitterness depends on boil gravity, kettle shape and hop age, so if you can send a sample for analysis once, do.

Lemon aroma can feel sharp. Brewers sometimes read it as sourness. It is not acidity, which comes from the pH of the beer. If your pale ale tastes tart, check the mash pH first. Aim for 5.2 to 5.6 measured at room temperature. For a gentler floral alternative when you want less zest, read our guide on Loral.

A moderate sulphate level in the water, with calcium around 100 mg/L, makes the hop edge crisper. A chloride-heavy water rounds it. Southern Cross suits the crisp side.
Blending with other pale ale hops

Southern Cross blends well with hops that add orange or stone fruit. Amarillo adds orange and flowers. Palisade pulls in apricot and a grassy edge. A 50/50 blend of Southern Cross and Amarillo in the whirlpool is a classic way to make a pale ale that tastes of citrus peel and flowers together.

A single hop batch first is still the best education. You learn what each hop does before you start layering.

Southern Cross reaches India through importers, often in vacuum packs. Check the crop year on the pack. Hops from last season that sat in a warm store will smell of old tea rather than lemon.

Once opened, reseal the pack, squeeze out the air and put it in the freezer. An ordinary kitchen zip bag lets in too much air. Use a heat-sealed foil or vacuum bag if you can. The same applies to every pellet hop you buy.
Why a single hop trial teaches you more

Brew your pale ale twice with the same grist and yeast. In batch one use Southern Cross only. In batch two use a blend. Taste both at the same age, ideally two weeks after packaging. Take notes on aroma intensity, bitterness quality and finish. The differences you notice in this one exercise will teach you more than reading ten hop descriptions.

Keep a simple log with the hop weight, the time of addition, the original gravity and the final gravity. Calculate alcohol by volume from your readings: ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25. A pale ale starting at 1.050 and finishing at 1.010 is about 5.3% ABV. Over a year, a log like this is how a homebrewer turns luck into repeatable beer.

Lemon and pine aroma fade first. A pale ale that tasted vivid at week two will taste dull by week eight if it has been kept warm. Serve it at 6 to 8 °C in a clean glass, with a proper head. A cold beer in a greasy glass loses its foam and most of its aroma.
faqs: What does Southern Cross taste like?
Lemon zest and pine resin with a light spice, less tropical than many modern hops.
Is Southern Cross a bittering or aroma hop?
Both. Alpha acids are in the low teens, so it bitters efficiently. The oils give a clean citrus aroma when added late.
Pale ale, golden ale and clean IPAs. It also works in a crisp lager when used late and in small amounts.
